_comment: Lodestar's colour lines (wave 13): rare asides, played by chart/prototype/colour.js, voice only, behind their own switch. A trigger lists what must be true for the line to fire; every key must match. `event` is the event kind (chart/EVENTS.md, plus the scheduler's own: g_well_top, posi_run, pulsar_string, fort_in_sight, lore, daystar_rise, radiation_start, radiation_end, nebula). Other keys match the event's data; a list matches any of its values; a `min_` prefix means at least; `count` is the nth event of that kind in the flight (for hi-fives and cups, the tally). Tick triggers: `flight_h` (whole earth hours flown), `clock` (the local hour it names, for an hour, from 21:00 to 05:00), `saturnight`, `date` (a day of the season calendar), `month` (its name, once a flight after 20 minutes), `fact` (a club fun fact: at most once a flight, in a quiet stretch 20 to 60 minutes in) and `quiet_s` (at least that many seconds without a line). Wave 20 added the categories `city` (on entering a town) and `club_fact`.

lines.text: Ninety-nine more and it's a Century.
Twenty light years. The Mission Debriefer will want that number.
Forty light years. That's about Worcester, as the crow flies.
Fifty light years. Halfway to a Century.
One hundred light years. There's a medal for that.
Twenty-six light years. A Boston Marathon, without the crowds.
Fifty light years. About Boston to Providence, by road.
Five light years. About the whole Southwest Corridor.
An earth hour already. That went quickly.
Two earth hours. That's a feature film, but outdoors.
One earth hour. Long enough for both sides of a mixtape.
Two earth hours. Long enough to have a favourite pulsar.
Five earth hours. Reykjavik is about that far, by plane.
Past eleven, and the lasers look their best.
Past midnight. Saturnight has become Sunstarday.
One in the morning. The city belongs to us and the raccoons.
Two in the morning. Luna 7-11 hours.
Past two. Nearly time for Dawn Patrol.
Daystar rising. The lasers can rest.
The daystar is up. You were here first.
Saturnight over Metro Alpha.
Nine o'clock on a Saturnight. Most missions haven't launched yet.
Four in the morning. The first buses are warming up.
Five in the morning. The daystar is on its way.
One in the morning. The pulsars are mostly talking to themselves.
That was a long posi g-well. Free light years.
Three black holes in one flight. A mission objective, some nights.
Crossing the Charles Asteroid Belt, the dry way.
Three hundred sixty-four smoots across, give or take an ear.
The Longfellow. Say hello to the salt and pepper shakers.
The Fort, up ahead. Home port.
Five quadrants. The Stellar Cartographer has some drawing to do.
Three constellations already. The Mission Leader may have views.
Five hi-fives. Fifteen bonus points, if anyone's counting.
Twenty-five hi-fives. Half the city has been greeted.
First cup crushed. Did it make a cool sound?
Three cups crushed. A tidy hat trick.
Fifty hi-fives. That's a parade.
Radiation. There's a points bonus for this, at least.
Radiation over. You flew right through it.
Radiation's stopped. No failure for radiation shortfall, then.
Nebula rolling in.
Nebula. The lasers are doing real work now.
Nebula. The pulsars glow in it.
April. The radiation is still on the cold side.
May. Lilac season at the Arboretum.
June. The daystar sets late, so the lasers come on late.
June. The fireflies are on the chart too, unofficially.
August. The cicadas have their own Life Support.
September. The students are back, and so are the moving trucks.
October. The flying salad is on the ground.
October. The spacesuits are getting thicker.
November. The lasers come on before dinner now.
January. Officially, the fleet is hibernating. You're not.
March. The potholes are in bloom.
February. The road salt gets everywhere, including the chain.
That little stone tower at Powder House is older than the country.
Along the Charles Asteroid Belt. Flat, and very pretty.
Harvard Constellation. The HONK! parade ends here.
Davis Constellation. The HONK! parade starts here.
Porter Constellation. The comet station under here is famously deep.
Porter Constellation. The big red sculpture turns in the wind.
The Minuteman Wormhole. Trains ran here, once.
The Minuteman. About ten light years of it, end to end.
The Minuteman. Fewer pulsars, more trees.
The Community Path. Comets for company, along part of it.
Fort Antwerp. Home since the Great Migration.
Tyler Street. The Fort stood here for about ten seasons.
Joy Street. A Fort stood here, for about a season.
Bunker Hill. The battle was mostly on Breed's Hill, to be fair.
The Arnold Arboretum. SCUL Day country.
Luna JP Licks. Ice cream molecules, by tradition.
The Pear. It's an oracle, if you have a question.
The space eggs. SCUL's number two destination.
Davis Constellation, named for Person Davis, a grain dealer.
Porter Constellation. The porterhouse steak may have been named here.
Harvard Constellation. The statue in the Yard is known for its three lies.
Union Constellation. Washington's army raised a flag on the hill above, in 1776.
Kenmore Constellation. The Citgo sign has watched over it since 1965.
Kenmore Constellation. One mile to go, if you're running the Marathon.
Nubian Constellation. It was Dudley Square until 2019.
The Pierre Lallement Path. He patented the pedal bicycle in 1866.
The Southwest Corridor was cleared for a highway that was never built.
The Kittie Knox Path. In 1895 she took on a whites-only cycling league.
Paul Dudley White was Eisenhower's heart doctor, and a great believer in bikes.
The Charles, once famously dirty. These days there's a public swim.
The Minuteman. Paul Revere rode out this way, more or less.
Alewife is named for a fish that still runs up the brook.
Fresh Pond. Cambridge drinks from this.
The Fens. Olmsted built a park here to fix a smelly marsh.
Jamaica Pond was left behind by a glacier.
At the BU Bridge, a boat, train, car and plane can stack up.
The Harvard Bridge. It goes to MIT, not Harvard.
Oliver Smoot, of the smoots, later ran the world's standards body.
The Harvard Bridge. MIT's dome once had a police car on top.
The Longfellow. The poet wrote about the bridge that stood here before.
The Anderson Bridge. A son built it in memory of his father.
Powder House. A raid on its gunpowder set off the 1774 Powder Alarm.
The Powder House was a windmill before it held gunpowder.
Back Bay. The cross streets run alphabetically, Arlington to Hereford.
Beacon Hill used to be taller. The top went into the Mill Pond.
The North End. In 1919, a wave of molasses came through here.
Charlestown. The oldest commissioned warship afloat is moored here.
Allston. On the first of September, the sidewalks fill with sofas.
Brighton. In the 1800s, this was Boston's cattle market.
Fenway. The ballpark opened five days after the Titanic sank.
Cambridgeport was laid out to be a port. It never quite was.
North Cambridge. Danehy Park used to be the city dump.
Coolidge Corner. John F. Kennedy was born a few blocks away.
Jamaica Plain. Harvard rents the Arboretum from Boston for a dollar a year.
South Boston. Dawn Patrol meets the daystar out on Castle Island.
East Boston. The airport is built on old harbour islands and fill.
Boston. Cows grazed on the Common until 1830.
Boston. America's first subway opened under Tremont Street in 1897.
Boston. America's first bicycle club started here, in 1878.
Boston. Albert Pope started selling Columbia bicycles here in the 1870s.
Cambridge. It was called Newtowne until 1638.
Cambridge. Necco wafers were made on Mass Ave for most of a century.
Somerville. It split off from Charlestown in 1842.
Somerville. Marshmallow Fluff was invented here, in 1917.
Somerville. Fort Summer, Fort Joy and Fort Tyler all stood here.
Brookline. It turned down joining Boston in 1873, and stayed out.
Watertown. The first Fort, Fort Francis, was here.
Watertown. The Army ran its Arsenal here for almost two centuries.
Arlington. Until 1867, it was called Menotomy.
Arlington. Samuel Wilson, the original Uncle Sam, was born here.
Medford. A plaque in town says Jingle Bells was written here.
Medford was famous for its rum, once.
Newton. Heartbreak Hill is in here somewhere.
Lexington. The Revolution's first shots were fired on its green.
Brookline. Frederick Law Olmsted lived and worked here.
Newton. A city of thirteen villages.
Lexington. The Minuteman runs right through the middle.
Alphamission. The space legs are coming back.
Alphamission. Cryogenic hibernation is over.
SCUL Day. The gang's orbital.
SCUL Day. Abandon All Hope flies again.
Century day. A hundred light years is the plan.
Century day. The intercept crew will be out late.
Founder's Day. Thirty-odd seasons, and it started with one ship.
HONK! weekend. Davis to Harvard, in parade formation.
Hallowheels. The one ride where civilians fly with us.
Hallowheels. The spacesuits are stranger than usual.
Omegamission. Last flight before hibernation.
Life Day. The Ode gets a new couplet.
SCUL Day. Peters Hill, then ice cream. The order is negotiable.
Hallowheels. Somebody is dressed as a civilian.
Omegamission. The awards are homemade, and so is the potluck.
Alphamission. Every year it gets a new pun for a name.
Century day. The bail points are planned, just in case.
Officially, SCUL stands for SCUL Can't Use Acronyms.
Skunk Day 50, in 2019, launched with seventeen Iron Cogs.
Catastrophe, the first flagship, weighs about a hundred and forty pounds.
The first flagship had a cassette stereo. Life Support, on tape.
Cloudbuster's mirror ball has a name: the Disco Death Star.
In SCUL, all droids are boys, and all ships are girls.
There's a set called the Seven Deadly Choppers. One is Pig Champion.
Skylab, the cursed ship, was retired on SCUL Day 2013.
One ship, Mjollnir, is titanium. Most are whatever was in the trash.
A cadet with no ship flies the Ghost Ship, on paper.
Ships are christened with PBR, spit, clam sauce, or mayonnaise.
Knightings call for a knightsaber. Sometimes the knightsaber is a plunger.
The founder himself wasn't formally knighted until 2017.
A civilian name costs one push-up. They add up over a whole career.
Every New Year, ranks reset and everyone is a maggot again.
Minus fifty for passing the navigator. Minus three thousand for a bad preflight.
Derby started with toilet-paper tails. Ribbons came later.
Some derbies are fought with cream pies. Some with sparklers.
At SCULimpics, anyone caught taking things seriously is disqualified.
Christmas in July means punting a plastic Santa. That's Kickin' Claus.
The bronze Pear in Dorchester honours a local pear, the Clapp's Favorite.
A SCUL time capsule was buried in 2012, and dug up in 2022.
SCUL was on PBS in 2007, on Design Squad.
Mission reports have been written as haiku, Lovecraft, and PHP code.
A mission can fail for visiting too many squares.
The Strength medal is known, unofficially, as the Medal of Stupid.
In 2013 a civilian shouted Bike-O-Ween, and the name stuck.
The Starchasers run Luna Libros, a costumed library tour.
SCUL has gone interuniversal: Montreal twice, and Lithuania.
Lithuania has its own chopper gang, the Raccoons.
Fort Antwerp is the seventh Fort, not counting the nomadic spell.
One of the taskforce jobs is Minister of Zoobs.
The Cadet Passport runs to thirteen pages.
It gets said at knightings: we're definitely not a cult.
The first SCUL Century, in 1998, was called Uranus Attack.
At Life Day, crowd-surfing is available on request.
The USB wing, the Universal Service Battalion, has built about forty-five ships.
The ship Golden Eagle is named after the founder's childhood gang.
Fleet formations include the pinwheel, the Flamingo and the Fourier.
At the Allston Rat Race, SCUL runs a chopper petting zoo.
SCUL has flown a mission for National Honeybee Day.
The radiobag became a radiobox, and then a radiobucket.
In the lingo, a toilet is a dark matter containment system.
A clothing failure, in the lingo, is a pantsical.
